newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: New boss for Air Afrique, rescue plan agreed.
newsitem.headline: New boss for Air Afrique, rescue plan agreed.

text.p: Air Afrique member states chose a former boss of Air Mauritius on Monday to run their struggling airline and agreed a plan to lift the burden of the multinational carrier's crippling debt.

Five heads of state and representatives from the six other member states nominated Sir Harry K. Tirvengadum of Mauritius to the post of managing director at a meeting in Ivory Coast's commercial capital Abidjan.
A communique issued at the end of the meeting announced plans to created a special company to take over responsibility for the planes at the root of Air Afrique's debt problem.

"The conference of the heads of state decided to create before December 31 1996 a patrimony company with a capital of 31 billion CFA francs... of which one of the missions will be to take over Air Afrique's plane-related debt," it said.
Each of the 11 members will provide one billion CFA of the capital with ASECNA-Service, a subsidiary of the multinational Francophone African air safety agency ASECNA, providing 20 billion CFA.
Tirvengadum was among candidates from a list presented by an international management consulting company. Sources close to the meeting said they included a French and a Belgian national.
Tirvengadum will replace Frenchman Yves-Roland Billecart, whose mandate at the head of the debt-plagued airline was cut short by the 11 Francophone member states.
Billecart's job, chairman and mangaing director, will be split between Tirvengadum and a chairman to be chosen at the next meeting of the company's board.
Air Afrique's owners see the airline, which was set up in 1961 during the heady days that followed independence from France, as a symbol of inter-African cooperation.

Host president, Ivory Coast's Henri Konan Bedie, told Monday's meeting draconian measures would be needed to ensure a lasting recovery of the airline, which serves West and Central Africa but also Europe, the United States and South Africa.

"First we must take all the necessary steps to ensure the (airline's) capacity to make significant (debt) repayments," Bedie said, noting that it had to pay 31 billion CFA in arrears by the end of December 1996.

He also called for recapitalisation of the airline, which has debts of around $400 million but lacks the operating revenue to ensure regular repayment. The debt relates to airliners bought soon after Billecart took over in 1989.
The 1994 devaluation of the CFA franc, used in many French-speaking countries in Africa, also undermined the airline's ability to repay its U.S. dollar-denominated debt.

Air Afrique, based in Abidjan, is majority-owned by Benin, Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Ivory Coast, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Senegal and Togo. Air France and other third parties also have a stake.
ASECNA, dominated by Air Afrique's members, had a windfall operating surplus. Its other members are Cameroon, Gabon, Madagascar and France.
